g12-economics-ue5-t1.overview: Taxation is the compulsory, unrequited payment citizens and firms make to government, and it funds most state activity in peacetime. This lesson defines taxation, explains the key terms and principles, and classifies taxes into direct and indirect.
objectives: Define taxation using the OECD terms compulsory and unrequited
Explain the macroeconomic and social objectives of taxation
State Adam Smith's canons and the modern principles of taxation
Describe the characteristics of a good tax system
Classify taxes into direct and indirect using impact and incidence
g12-economics-ue5-t1.simple: A tax is a compulsory, unrequited payment to general government. Compulsory means it must be paid because the law says so; unrequited means the taxpayer gets nothing direct in return. Taxes raise revenue for administration, law and order, defence, infrastructure and public services, and they help redistribute income and discourage harmful goods. Taxes are described by their rate, base, incidence, impact and effect. Adam Smith set out famous canons of taxation such as equity, certainty, convenience and economy, and a good tax system is simple, adequate, elastic and administratively efficient. Taxes are either direct, where the burden falls on the person who pays, or indirect, where the burden can be shifted to someone else.
g12-economics-ue5-t1.detailed:
What a tax is. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) defines a tax as a compulsory, unrequited payment to general government. Compulsory means taxes are not voluntary purchase payments but mandatory impositions, payable in line with what is legislated; to enforce this, governments use constitutions, proclamations, regulations and directives. Unrequited means the benefits government provides to a taxpayer are not in proportion to the payments made, so tax is levied without a quid pro quo, without anything in direct return. Taxation is not the only source of government revenue - there is also borrowing, fees for services and printing money - but taxation typically accounts for 90 percent or more of total governmental receipts in times of peace.

Why governments tax. In minimalist terms, governments impose taxes for three basic purposes: to cover the cost of administration, to maintain law and order and to defend the public. They also tax to fund economic infrastructure, health facilities, transport, education, telecom and electricity, and to provide facilities for less able members of society. Beyond revenue, taxation helps provide public goods, promotes redistribution of income and wealth, and discourages consumption of harmful goods (demerit goods with negative externalities such as cigarettes and alcohol). The objectives list also includes stabilizing the economy, encouraging capital formation, reducing regional imbalance, enhancing living standards, directing scarce resources to essential goods, and minimizing unemployment while encouraging exports.

Key terminology. Tax rate is the per-unit amount or the percentage rate at which the economic activity is taxed. Tax base is the level or quantity of the economic activity that is taxed; a higher tax rate reduces the tax base because it makes the activity less attractive. Tax incidence concerns how the burden is distributed among economic units; it is the final resting place of the tax, found by seeing who is made worse off and by how much. Impact of a tax is its first point of contact with the taxpayer, felt by whoever bears the first statutory responsibility for paying it. Effect of a tax refers to the responses of taxpayers and the economy, influencing production, growth, saving, investment and inequality.

Principles of taxation. In the Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith proposed the canons of taxation: every subject should contribute in proportion to his ability; the tax each must pay should be certain, not arbitrary, with the time, manner and quantity to be paid clear and plain; every tax should be levied at the time and in the manner most convenient to the contributor; every tax should take as little as possible out of people's pockets over and above what it brings into the public treasury; the cost of collection should be minimal (the canon of economy); and the system should yield enough revenue that government is not forced into deficit financing (the canon of fiscal adequacy). Modern principles add that a tax system should not distort the optimal allocation of factors in efficient markets, should be fair, a flexible automatic stabilizer, clear and transparent, definitive and inexpensive to collect.

Characteristics of a good tax system. Taxation is compulsory (non-payment is a criminal offense), revenues are spent on collective use serving a common interest, taxes are paid regularly with known due dates, and taxes are levied on all people without discrimination yet according to ability to pay. A good tax system is simple, financially adequate and elastic; broad based, taxing not only income but also property and commodities; administratively efficient; balanced and harmonious; it reduces economic inequalities, ensures economic stability, raises the standard of living, acts as an instrument of economic growth, is socially advantageous and enables optimum allocation of resources. In short, a good tax system must be both equitable and efficient.

Classification and world examples. Based on impact or incidence there are two major types. Direct taxes impose impact and incidence on the same person who earns the income; they are computed on ability to pay, and include employee income tax, business income tax, rental income tax, agricultural income tax, poll tax, land tax, property tax, royalty tax, capital gains tax, gift tax and inheritance tax, further divided into income tax, transfer tax (commonly levied on real estate and the taxable property of a deceased person), property tax (charged on land and buildings) and capital gains tax (charged when assets such as stocks, real estate or a business are sold, computed from the acquisition and selling amounts). Indirect taxes impose impact and incidence on different persons; examples are VAT, excise tax, turnover tax, surtax, customs duty and stamp duty. In the UK, the main taxes include income tax with a basic rate of 20 percent on income above a threshold of 11,500 pounds, national insurance contributions, consumption tax (VAT at 17.5 percent), excise duties on alcohol and tobacco, corporation tax and stamp duty, plus a sin tax on tobacco, alcohol, sugar-added drinks and gambling. In the USA the five most common taxes are payroll tax, individual income tax, corporate income tax, wealth taxes and consumption taxes, the first four being direct; the US federal government gets 41.6 percent of its tax revenue from individual income tax, 34.8 percent from payroll taxes and 15.1 percent from corporate income tax (Gruber, 2015).

keyTerms.def: A compulsory, unrequited payment to general government, levied by law without anything given directly in return.
The per-unit amount or the percentage rate at which the economic activity is taxed.
The level or quantity of an economic activity that is taxed; higher tax rates generally shrink the base.
The distribution of the burden of a tax; its final resting place, determined by who is made worse off.
The tax's first point of contact with the taxpayer, borne by those with the first statutory duty to pay.
The responses of taxpayers and the economy to the tax, affecting production, growth, saving, investment and inequality.
A tax whose impact and incidence fall on the same person who earns the income, assessed on ability to pay.
A tax whose impact and incidence fall on different persons, such as VAT, excise tax and customs duty.

workedExamples.problem: The US federal government draws 41.6 percent of tax revenue from individual income tax, 34.8 percent from payroll taxes and 15.1 percent from corporate income tax. These three direct taxes together supply what share of federal tax revenue?
workedExamples.given: Individual income tax = 41.6%; payroll tax = 34.8%; corporate income tax = 15.1%.
workedExamples.formula: Direct tax share = individual income share + payroll share + corporate income share.
workedExamples.answer: About 91.5 percent of US federal tax revenue comes from these three direct taxes, leaving only a small share from consumption and other taxes.

workedExamples.problem: Classify each tax as direct or indirect using the impact and incidence test: employee income tax, VAT, property tax, customs duty, capital gains tax.
workedExamples.given: Five taxes: three on income or property of the payer, two on transactions.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a direct tax puts impact and incidence on the same person; an indirect tax puts them on different persons.
workedExamples.substitution: Employee income tax, property tax and capital gains tax are assessed on the income or property of the person who pays; VAT and customs duty are collected at transactions and their burden can rest on consumers.
workedExamples.calculation: Taxes on income and property pass the same-person test, so they are direct; taxes collected at sale and import pass through to others, so they are indirect.
workedExamples.answer: Direct: employee income tax, property tax, capital gains tax. Indirect: VAT, customs duty.

workedExamples.problem: In peacetime taxation accounts for 90 percent or more of total governmental receipts. If a government collects total receipts of 200 billion birr, what is the minimum amount expected from taxation?
workedExamples.given: Total governmental receipts = 200 billion birr; tax share is 90 percent or more.
workedExamples.formula: Minimum tax revenue = 90% of total receipts.
workedExamples.substitution: Minimum tax revenue = 0.90 x 200 billion birr.
workedExamples.answer: At least 180 billion birr should come from taxation, though borrowing, fees and money printing supply the rest.

commonMistakes: Thinking a tax is a price for a specific service, when in fact it is compulsory and unrequited with no direct return.
Confusing tax incidence (final resting place) with impact (first point of contact).
Believing taxation is the only source of government revenue, ignoring borrowing, fees and money creation.
Mixing up direct and indirect taxes by assuming all taxes on goods are direct.
Forgetting that a higher tax rate usually shrinks the tax base by making the activity less attractive.
Listing certainty or convenience as objectives of taxation when they are principles (canons) of taxation.
Assuming a good tax system needs only to raise revenue, ignoring equity and efficiency.
applications: Recognising that the salary income tax withheld by an employer in Ethiopia is a direct tax whose burden stays with the worker.
Explaining why excise tax on cigarettes and alcohol is used to discourage harmful consumption while raising revenue.
Comparing Ethiopia's scheduled income taxes with the UK's 20 percent basic rate and the USA's payroll and income taxes.
Using tax incidence analysis to judge whether a new import duty will finally rest on importers or on consumers.
Appraising Ethiopia's tax system against Adam Smith's canons such as certainty, convenience and economy.
Arguing that a tax is legitimate only when backed by legislation such as proclamations, regulations and directives.
g12-economics-ue5-t1.summary: A tax is a compulsory, unrequited payment to general government that typically supplies 90 percent or more of receipts in peacetime and serves revenue, redistribution and regulatory objectives. Adam Smith's canons and the modern principles demand equity, certainty, convenience and economy from a system that should be simple, adequate, elastic and administratively efficient. Taxes divide into direct taxes, whose burden rests on the income earner, and indirect taxes such as VAT, excise and customs duty, whose burden can be shifted.

g12-economics-ue5-t2.overview: How should the tax load be shared fairly? This lesson compares the benefits approach with the ability-to-pay approach and shows how progressive, proportional and regressive taxes classify taxes by their impact on income groups.
objectives: State the benefits approach to tax equity and its main limitation
Explain the ability-to-pay approach and the questions it raises
Distinguish horizontal equity from vertical equity
Define progressive, proportional and regressive taxes in terms of the average tax rate
Classify a tax as progressive, proportional or regressive from tax payment data
g12-economics-ue5-t2.simple: There are two approaches to tax equity. The benefits approach says each taxpayer should contribute according to the benefits received from public services, but about half of government spending, such as on the army or courts, cannot be traced to specific beneficiaries. The ability-to-pay approach says taxes should be distributed according to the taxpayer's capacity to pay, calling for horizontal equity (equal people pay equal taxes) and vertical equity (the unequal treated unequally). Taxes are then classified by impact: a progressive tax sees the average rate rise with income, a proportional tax keeps the average rate the same at all income levels, and a regressive tax lets the average rate fall as income rises.
g12-economics-ue5-t2.detailed:
The benefits approach. Under the benefits approach, an equitable tax system is one in which each taxpayer contributes in line with the benefits he or she receives from public services. The aim is to work out how much each person gains from public spending. Its great advantage is that it links tax equity to the expenditure side of the public budget. However, it is much easier to state this abstract basis than to apply it: while spending on health, education and social subsidies can be attributed to beneficiary households, about half of government spending cannot be. It is difficult, if not impossible, to determine who benefits most from spending on the army, police, diplomatic service or judicial system.

The ability-to-pay approach. Here tax is levied on each taxpayer in line with his or her ability to pay, so the approach focuses on the distributive nature of taxation. People with equal capacity should pay the same, and people with greater ability should pay more. Three questions arise: how to measure ability to pay, how to set a fair set of tax rates for differing abilities, and how to compare the economic status of different taxpayers. Ideally the measure would reflect the entire welfare a person can derive from consumption (present and future), holding of wealth and enjoyment of leisure, but such a comprehensive measure is not practicable.

Horizontal and vertical equity. The ability-to-pay approach rests on two equity ideas. Horizontal equity means people in the same circumstances pay the same taxes. Vertical equity means unequals should be treated unequally, with a degree of proportionality so that larger ability bears a larger burden. Together they answer the classroom question of whether the rich should pay more: under the ability-to-pay view, they should.

Classifying taxes by impact. The concepts of progressive, proportional and regressive taxes (called type by impact by Greenlaw and Taylor, 2017) operationalize vertical equity. A progressive tax is one where those with higher incomes pay a higher share of taxes out of their income than those with lower incomes; the average tax rate rises with income. A proportional tax takes the same share from everyone regardless of income level; the average tax rate is the same at all income levels. A regressive tax takes a lower share from high-income people than from low-income people; the average tax rate falls when income rises.

Ethiopian application. Ethiopia's employment income tax applies rates ranging from 10 percent to 35 percent, with the higher rate charged at higher earnings; as the average rate rises with income, this schedule is progressive and expresses vertical equity. Understanding the type by impact matters because it determines who finally bears the relative burden: a regressive tax places a proportionally heavier load on the poor even if the rich pay more in absolute birr.

keyTerms.def: Fairness in distributing the tax burden among taxpayers.
The principle that tax obligations should be based on the benefits received from public services.
The principle that taxes should be distributed according to each taxpayer's capacity to pay.
People in the same circumstances paying the same taxes.
Treating unequals unequally, so those with greater ability pay proportionally more.
A tax whose average rate rises with income, so higher earners pay a higher share of their income.
A tax whose average rate is the same at all income levels.
A tax whose average rate falls as income rises, so higher earners pay a lower share of their income.

workedExamples.problem: Ayele has an income of 4,000 birr and pays tax of 300 birr, while Atote has an income of 20,000 birr and pays tax of 1,400 birr. Is this tax progressive, proportional or regressive?
workedExamples.given: Ayele: income 4,000 birr, tax 300 birr. Atote: income 20,000 birr, tax 1,400 birr.
workedExamples.formula: Average tax rate = tax paid / income; the tax is progressive if the average rate rises with income, regressive if it falls.
workedExamples.substitution: Ayele's average rate = 300 / 4,000; Atote's average rate = 1,400 / 20,000.
workedExamples.calculation: 300 / 4,000 = 0.075 = 7.5%; 1,400 / 20,000 = 0.07 = 7.0%. The average rate falls from 7.5% to 7.0% as income rises.
workedExamples.answer: The tax is regressive, because the higher earner pays a smaller percentage of income in tax.

workedExamples.problem: Suppose a worker earning 1,000 birr pays 100 birr in tax and a manager earning 10,000 birr pays 1,500 birr. Classify the tax by impact.
workedExamples.given: Low earner: income 1,000 birr, tax 100 birr. High earner: income 10,000 birr, tax 1,500 birr.
workedExamples.formula: Average tax rate = tax paid / income; compare the two rates.
workedExamples.calculation: 100 / 1,000 = 10%; 1,500 / 10,000 = 15%. The average rate rises with income.
workedExamples.answer: The tax is progressive: higher-income people pay a higher share of their income.

workedExamples.problem: A flat tax takes exactly 15 percent of every taxpayer's income, whatever the level. What type is it, and does it satisfy horizontal equity?
workedExamples.given: Average rate is 15 percent at every income level.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a proportional tax has the same average rate at all income levels.
workedExamples.substitution: A person earning 2,000 birr pays 300 birr; a person earning 20,000 birr pays 3,000 birr; both pay 15 percent.
workedExamples.calculation: Both pay the same share, so the average rate does not change with income; equals in ability are treated equally.
workedExamples.answer: It is a proportional tax, and it satisfies horizontal equity because people in the same circumstances pay the same share.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia taxes employment income at rates ranging from 10 to 35 percent. Which tax-equity concept does this rate structure express, and why?
workedExamples.given: Schedule A rates range from 10 percent to 35 percent of employment income.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: vertical equity means unequals should be treated unequally, so rates should rise with ability to pay.
workedExamples.substitution: Low earners face the 10 percent end of the range and high earners the 35 percent end.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the rate rises with earnings, the average tax burden grows with ability to pay.
workedExamples.answer: Vertical equity, implemented through a progressive employment income tax.

commonMistakes: Judging progressivity by the absolute birr amount paid instead of by the percentage of income (average rate).
Assuming that when a rich person pays more birr than a poor person the tax is automatically progressive.
Confusing horizontal equity (equals treated equally) with vertical equity (unequals treated unequally).
Believing the benefits approach can measure who benefits from every kind of spending, when about half of spending cannot be attributed.
Calling a regressive tax one where the rich pay less in total birr, when the point is that they pay a smaller share of income.
Forgetting that only proportional taxes keep the average rate constant at all income levels.
applications: Using the 10 to 35 percent employment income tax range to show classmates why Ethiopian salary tax is progressive.
Applying the benefits approach when analysing fees for a service users can clearly identify, and noting why it fails for defence spending.
Computing average tax rates for two earners to decide whether a proposed tax is fair to low-income households.
Explaining to a market trader why a fixed tax per transaction may be regressive against small vendors.
Using vertical equity to argue why large business profits should bear a larger percentage than small incomes.
Recognising that tax knowledge and fairness perception shape voluntary compliance, as the textbook notes.
g12-economics-ue5-t2.summary: Tax equity can be pursued through the benefits approach, which links tax to received public services but fails where spending cannot be traced, or through the ability-to-pay approach built on horizontal and vertical equity. By impact, a tax is progressive when the average rate rises with income, proportional when it is constant, and regressive when it falls. Ethiopia's employment income tax rates of 10 to 35 percent are a progressive application of vertical equity.

g12-economics-ue5-t3.overview: Ethiopia's tax system has evolved from a 1944 agricultural decree into a scheduled income tax system run by the Ministry of Revenues. This lesson covers the constitutional framework, the income tax schedules, and the indirect taxes and tax accounting practices of Ethiopia.
objectives: Trace the historical development of Ethiopia's tax system from 1944 to the present
Explain the constitutional sharing of revenue between federal and regional governments
Describe the five schedules of income under Tax Proclamation 286/2002
Compute obligations under VAT, TOT, surtax, withholding and pension contributions using official rates
Explain the link between accounting records and the determination of tax liability
g12-economics-ue5-t3.simple: Ethiopia introduced income taxation in 1944, when the Emperor decreed that peasants pay one-tenth of their agricultural products to tax officials. Today the Ministry of Revenues collects taxes under the FDRE Constitution, which lets federal and regional governments share revenue sources. Under Tax Proclamation 286/2002 income falls into schedules: A (employment, taxed 10 to 35 percent and withheld by employers), B (rental of buildings), C (business), D (other income) and E (exempt income). Indirect taxes include VAT at a 15 percent standard rate since 2003, turnover tax of 2 or 10 percent, excise tax on 19 groups of goods, a 10 percent surtax on imports, withholding tax of 2 percent, stamp duty and customs duty. Accounting records supply the figures from which tax liabilities are calculated.
g12-economics-ue5-t3.detailed:
History and institutions. Ethiopia introduced income taxation in 1944, when the Emperor issued a decree requiring all peasants to pay one-tenth of their agricultural products to tax officials; tax regimes have changed with changes of government since then. Currently the federal Ministry of Revenues (MoR) is responsible for tax collection. It prepares decrees, directives and regulations on fiscal policy matters and submits them for parliament to legislate. As a federal country, Ethiopia's constitution allows revenue sharing between federal and regional governments.

Legal framework. The legal framework is provided by Proclamation No. 33/1992 and the FDRE Constitution (1995), which promulgated sharing of revenue between federal and regional governments. The federal government levies taxes and collects duties on revenue sources reserved to it and draws up, approves and administers the federal budget (Article 51(10)). Regional states levy and collect taxes and duties on sources reserved to the states and administer their own budgets (Article 52(2(e))). As of April 2022 Ethiopia has 11 regional states plus 2 autonomous administrations, Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa Cities.

The five schedules. Under Tax Proclamation No. 286/2002 and Regulations No. 78/2002 there are four schedules of income in addition to exempt income. Schedule A covers income from employment, taxed at rates ranging from 10 to 35 percent; it is withheld by employers and is a final tax, so employees earning income exclusively from employment need not declare it. Employment income includes salary, wages, allowances, bonus, commission, gratuity, the value of fringe benefits, and payments on termination such as redundancy compensation or a golden handshake. Schedule B covers income from rental of buildings; taxable income is the gross rental amount reduced by allowed deductions. Schedule C covers business income, also taxed after allowed deductions. Schedule D covers other income: royalties, income paid for services rendered outside Ethiopia, income from games, dividends, casual rental of property, interest and specified non-business capital gains. Schedule E lists exempt income, including the cost of medical treatment of employees, hardship allowance, salary of domestic servants, maintenance or child support payments, travelling expenses of employees recruited from elsewhere, pension contribution and compensation payments.

VAT. Value added tax is levied on the value added at different stages and is a sales tax administered in a different form. Ethiopia introduced the VAT Act on 1 January 2003 with a standard rate of 15 percent on every taxable transaction by a registered person; VAT must be included in the selling price of every taxable supply by a vendor (a person registered or required to be registered for VAT). VAT is destination-based, a consumption tax, so only consumption is taxed. On exempt supplies the supplier charges no output tax but must still bear input VAT on purchases.

TOT, excise and surtax. Turnover tax is an equalization tax imposed on persons not registered for VAT; VAT registration is limited to those whose annual transactions exceed 500,000 Birr. For services rendered locally the rate is 2 percent on contractors, grain mills, tractors and combine harvesters, and 10 percent on others. Excise tax applies to selected goods, luxury items and demand-inelastic basic goods, and to goods hazardous to health; it covers 19 groups of items and 378 goods, with rates from 5 to 500 percent, payable at customs clearing on imports and not later than 30 days from the date of production for locally produced goods (EIC, 2020). Surtax is an additional 10 percent on imported goods except fertilizers, petroleum and lubricants, motor vehicles for freight, passengers and special purposes, aircraft, spacecraft and parts thereof, and capital (investment) goods; the Ministry of Finance may adjust the exempt list.

Pension, withholding, stamp and customs. Contributions to the Private Organizations Pension Fund are based on the employee's salary, paid 11 percent by the employer and 7 percent by the employee. Withholding tax of 2 percent of the value of domestic transactions is deducted by all bodies and specified sole proprietor businesses and remitted monthly. Stamp duty is imposed on services rendered through affixing official seals or marks on documents, indicating that a required tax has been paid. Customs duty is imposed on imported or exported goods and is the best instrument to prevent or reduce importation, serving as a trade barrier; rates may reach 100 percent or above, which protects infant domestic industries from stiff competition with subsidized foreign importers.

Tax and accounting. Tax and accounting are two separate entities that are also linked: all taxation involves accounting processes, the practice of calculating financial statements and figures, and those statements are used to make tax calculations. Tax accounting is used by individuals, businesses and other entities. For an individual it focuses on income, qualifying deductions and any investment gains or losses; individuals employed in public establishments in Ethiopia have their income tax paid by their employers. Businesses must keep up-to-date financial records to determine their tax liabilities.

keyTerms.def: The federal agency responsible for tax collection in Ethiopia; it drafts fiscal decrees, directives and regulations for parliament to legislate.
Under Proclamation 286/2002, a category of income for tax purposes: A employment, B rental, C business, D other income, E exempt.
An indirect consumption tax of 15 percent on value added at each stage, introduced in Ethiopia on 1 January 2003.
An equalization tax of 2 or 10 percent on persons not registered for VAT, completing coverage of the tax system.
A tax on selected luxury and demand-inelastic goods, covering 19 groups and 378 goods at rates from 5 to 500 percent.
An additional 10 percent tax on imported goods, with exemptions such as fertilizers and capital goods.
A 2 percent deduction on the value of domestic transactions, remitted monthly to the tax authority.
Income listed in Schedule E that is not taxed, such as medical treatment costs, hardship allowance and pension contributions.

workedExamples.problem: An employee in a private organization earns a monthly salary of 5,000 Birr. Compute the pension contributions to the Private Organizations Pension Fund for the employee and the employer.
workedExamples.given: Monthly salary = 5,000 Birr; employee contribution rate = 7%; employer contribution rate = 11%.
workedExamples.answer: The employee contributes 350 Birr and the employer 550 Birr, a total of 900 Birr per month; pension contribution is also exempt income under Schedule E.

workedExamples.problem: A registered vendor sells taxable goods for 10,000 Birr. VAT at Ethiopia's standard rate applies. What output VAT must the vendor account for?
workedExamples.given: Taxable supply value = 10,000 Birr; VAT standard rate = 15%.
workedExamples.formula: VAT = taxable amount x standard VAT rate.
workedExamples.answer: The vendor charges 1,500 Birr output VAT on the 10,000 Birr taxable supply, VAT being a 15 percent destination-based consumption tax.

workedExamples.problem: Two unregistered service providers each render local services worth 20,000 Birr in a month: one is a contractor, the other an ordinary service provider. Compare their turnover tax (TOT).
workedExamples.given: Service value = 20,000 Birr each; TOT rate = 2% on contractors, grain mills, tractors and combine harvesters; 10% on others.
workedExamples.formula: TOT = value of services x applicable TOT rate.
workedExamples.answer: The contractor pays 400 Birr while the other provider pays 2,000 Birr, because TOT charges 2 percent on contractors and 10 percent on other local services.

workedExamples.problem: A trading company concludes a domestic transaction with a value of 50,000 Birr. Calculate the withholding tax it must deduct and remit.
workedExamples.given: Transaction value = 50,000 Birr; withholding rate = 2% of transaction value.
workedExamples.answer: The company deducts 1,000 Birr and remits it to the tax authority monthly, as required for withholding on domestic transactions.

commonMistakes: Believing Ethiopia's income taxation began in 2002, when in fact the first income tax decree dates to 1944.
Assuming employees must declare their income when all their earnings come from employment, since Schedule A tax is withheld and is a final tax.
Calling VAT an origin-based tax, when the textbook stresses it is destination-based, taxing only consumption.
Mixing up the TOT rates, 2 percent for contractors, grain mills, tractors and combine harvesters and 10 percent for others.
Forgetting that surtax exempts fertilizers, petroleum and lubricants, certain motor vehicles, aircraft and capital goods, not just luxury items.
Reversing the pension contribution shares, which are 11 percent from the employer and 7 percent from the employee.
Thinking tax and accounting are unrelated, when accounting statements are exactly what tax calculations are built on.
applications: Checking whether a business you know exceeds the 500,000 Birr annual transaction threshold and so must register for VAT rather than pay TOT.
Using the Schedule A withholding rule to explain why a salaried worker's payslip shows tax deducted before payment.
Applying the excise tax rationale of 5 to 500 percent rates to argue a health case for raising prices of hazardous goods.
Noting that a rental property owner reports gross rental income less allowed deductions under Schedule B.
Observing that imported machinery for an investment project may escape the 10 percent surtax as a capital good.
Encouraging a small business to keep up-to-date financial records so its Schedule C tax liability can be correctly determined.
g12-economics-ue5-t3.summary: Ethiopia's tax system grew from the 1944 decree on peasant produce into a constitutionally shared federal-regional system administered by the Ministry of Revenues under Proclamations 33/1992 and 286/2002. Income is taxed through Schedules A to E, with employment income taxed at 10 to 35 percent and withheld as a final tax, while VAT (15 percent), TOT (2 and 10 percent), excise (5 to 500 percent), surtax (10 percent), withholding (2 percent), stamp and customs duties make up the indirect taxes. Accounting records feed the calculations from which every liability is determined.

events.label: First income tax decree
events.detail: Emperor's decree requires peasants to pay one-tenth of their agricultural products to tax officials.

events.label: Proclamation No. 33/1992
events.detail: Provides the legal framework for tax and revenue sharing between federal and regional governments.

events.label: FDRE Constitution
events.detail: Federal government levies federal taxes (Art. 51(10)); regional states levy their reserved taxes (Art. 52(2(e))).

events.label: Proclamation 286/2002 and Regulations 78/2002
events.detail: Establish the five schedules of income, the Excise Tax Proclamation 307/2002 and related rules.

events.label: VAT Act begins
events.detail: VAT is introduced on 1 January 2003 with a standard rate of 15 percent.

It applies to 19 groups of items and 378 goods with rates from 5% to 500%
It is payable only on exports

questions.explanation: Surtax applies to imported goods except fertilizers, petroleum and lubricants, certain motor vehicles, aircraft, spacecraft and capital goods.

questions.answer: all taxation involves accounting processes|financial statements are used to make tax calculations|records determine tax liability
questions.explanation: Taxation involves accounting processes: financial statements and figures are used for the tax calculations, and businesses keep records to determine liabilities.

g12-economics-ue5-t4.overview: Tax systems everywhere are criticised for complex administration and for being hard to understand and comply with. This lesson explains how those failures breed tax avoidance and tax evasion, and the specific problems and remedies for tax administration in Ethiopia.
objectives: Explain why complexity of administration and compliance difficulty generate wider costs
Define tax compliance and describe its main forms of failure
Distinguish tax avoidance from tax evasion and state its legal status of each
Give the two reasons the underground economy exists
Suggest remedial actions for the problems of taxation in developing countries including Ethiopia
g12-economics-ue5-t4.simple: Tax systems face heavy criticism for complexity of administration and the difficulty taxpayers have in understanding and complying with the law. Both raise the cost of calculating tax correctly, and this pushes some people into the underground economy: unreported transactions (tax evasion) and tax shelters (tax avoidance). Tax avoidance means legally arranging one's affairs to minimise tax using exemptions, deductions and incentives; evasion means falsifying returns or not filing at all, which is illegal. In developing countries like Ethiopia the problems include perceived corruption, compliance costs, weak fairness perception and limited tax knowledge. Remedies include simplifying rules, modernising customer service with client orientation, cutting assessment and collection costs, and improving management.
g12-economics-ue5-t4.detailed:
Global criticisms of tax systems. Major criticisms around the world focus on the complexity of tax administration and the difficulty taxpayers have in understanding and complying with it. Both problems cause taxpayers to incur costs simply to calculate their tax liability correctly. A complex system also encourages the growth of unreported transactions in the underground economy (tax evasion) and the growth of demand for tax shelters (tax avoidance). In developed countries, a main tool for improving efficiency is to modernise customer services, applying new management techniques built on the concepts of client orientation or customer orientation.

Problems in developing countries. In developing countries, including Ethiopia, tax systems face diverse problems: the complexity of the tax system, perception of corruption, the cost of compliance, the fairness perception of the tax system, and tax knowledge. Tax knowledge matters because it has a positive effect on voluntary tax compliance - the better taxpayers understand the system, the more willingly they comply. Broadly, these problems fall under two headings: tax compliance and bureaucracy in the tax system.

Compliance and non-compliance. Problems related to tax compliance are the biggest problems faced by any tax administration. Tax compliance refers to the degree to which taxpayers comply with the tax laws. On the contrary, tax non-compliance takes the form of tax avoidance and tax evasion, and both shrink the revenue available for public services.

Tax avoidance versus tax evasion. Tax avoidance means arranging one's affairs so as to minimise the tax burden, taking full advantage of the provisions of the tax code or schedule to reduce one's obligations - for example, reducing the burden through exemptions, deductions or incentives approved in the tax schedule. From the perspective of law, tax avoidance is not illegal, though it poses problems for tax administration. Tax evasion means falsifying information on a tax return to reduce one's liability, or even not filing at all (failing to pay legally due taxes), which is illegal.

The underground economy. Tax evasion is rooted in underground economic activities that exist for at least two reasons. First, certain activities are themselves illegal, so individuals do not want any record that those activities took place. Second, high marginal tax rates give people an incentive to obtain income without reporting it. Both forces hide economic activity from the tax authority and erode the tax base.

Other administrative problems and remedies. Tax administrations in Ethiopia and elsewhere also face a steadily growing workload, the complexity of fiscal legislation, the attitude of taxpayers and the degree of non-compliance, the need to improve customer service, the need to reduce the costs of tax assessment and collection, and the need for efficient and effective management. These raise questions of how collection can be made more efficient and effective - which is why modernised, client-oriented service and simpler, more transparent rules are emphasised as remedies.

keyTerms.def: The degree to which taxpayers comply with the tax laws.
Failure to comply with tax laws, taking the form of tax avoidance and tax evasion.
Legally arranging one's affairs to minimise the tax burden using exemptions, deductions or incentives in the tax schedule.
Illegally falsifying information on a tax return, or not filing at all, to avoid paying legally due taxes.
A legal arrangement approved in the tax code that reduces a taxpayer's burden, fuelling demand under avoidance.
Unreported economic activity, generated by illegal activities or high marginal tax rates that reward non-reporting.
The cost taxpayers incur to correctly calculate and pay their tax liability.
A modern tax-administration philosophy that treats taxpayers as customers to be served efficiently.

workedExamples.problem: Taxpayer X claims every exemption and deduction approved in the tax schedule to reduce her bill. Taxpayer Y falsifies his sales figures on his return and under-reports income. Classify each behaviour and state its legal status.
workedExamples.given: X uses approved exemptions, deductions and incentives. Y falsifies information on a tax return.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: using provisions of the tax schedule is avoidance (not illegal); falsifying information or not filing is evasion (illegal).
workedExamples.substitution: X takes full advantage of the provisions of the tax code, so her conduct fits the definition of avoidance. Y falsifies information, which fits the definition of evasion.
workedExamples.calculation: Avoidance is not illegal from the perspective of law but burdens administration; evasion is illegal.
workedExamples.answer: X is practising tax avoidance (legal); Y is practising tax evasion, which is a crime.

workedExamples.problem: A country sharply raises marginal tax rates on reported income. Predict the effect on the underground economy and name the mechanism the textbook gives for it.
workedExamples.given: Marginal tax rates on reported income increase sharply.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: high marginal tax rates give people an incentive to obtain income without reporting it.
workedExamples.substitution: Since unreported income escapes the now-higher marginal rate, the reward for hiding income rises.
workedExamples.calculation: More taxpayers choose not to report, so unreported transactions grow and the tax base shrinks even though rates rose.
workedExamples.answer: The underground economy grows, driven by the incentive of high marginal tax rates to keep income unreported; this is why evasion rises even when rates do.

workedExamples.problem: A tax office in a developing country is seen as corrupt and publishes rules taxpayers cannot understand. Explain, using the textbook factors, what happens to voluntary compliance and how the office can respond.
workedExamples.given: Problems present: complexity of the tax system, perception of corruption, fairness perception and tax knowledge.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: complexity and perceived unfairness or corruption raise compliance costs and lower voluntary compliance, while tax knowledge raises it.
workedExamples.substitution: Taxpayers face higher costs to calculate liability correctly and less trust, so compliance falls and evasion tempting; some shift to legal shelters.
workedExamples.calculation: Remedies follow from the causes: modernise customer service with client orientation, simplify the rules, cut assessment and collection costs, and raise taxpayer knowledge.
workedExamples.answer: Voluntary compliance falls; the office should simplify administration, improve client-oriented customer service and taxpayer education to rebuild fairness perception and compliance.

commonMistakes: Thinking tax avoidance is illegal, when the textbook states it is not illegal from the perspective of law.
Thinking tax evasion is merely clever planning, when it is falsifying information or not filing, which is illegal.
Assuming tax evasion grows only from greed and ignoring the two roots: illegal activities and high marginal tax rates.
Believing complexity harms only the tax office, when it also costs taxpayers dearly to calculate liability correctly.
Forgetting that tax knowledge positively affects voluntary tax compliance, so taxpayer education is a remedy.
Confusing tax compliance itself with its failures; compliance is the degree to which taxpayers follow the tax laws.
Assuming developed and developing countries face identical tax problems; Ethiopia's include perceived corruption and weak fairness perception.
applications: File honest returns for a family business rather than under-reporting sales, since evasion is illegal.
Using only exemptions and deductions approved in the Ethiopian tax schedule, which is legal avoidance, and never falsifying figures.
Explaining to peers why an underground market of unreported trade ultimately starves schools and clinics of funding.
Advocating simpler tax forms and client-oriented counters at the local revenue office to cut compliance costs.
Supporting tax-awareness clubs in your locality, since taxpayer knowledge improves voluntary compliance.
Arguing that lowering excessive marginal rates can reduce the incentive to keep income unreported.
g12-economics-ue5-t4.summary: Tax systems worldwide are criticised for administrative complexity and compliance difficulty, which raise compliance costs and push activity into the underground economy. Non-compliance appears as tax avoidance, the legal use of exemptions, deductions and incentives, and tax evasion, the illegal falsification or non-filing of returns, rooted in illegal activities and high marginal tax rates. In Ethiopia the biggest problems are complexity, perceived corruption, compliance costs, fairness perception and limited tax knowledge, addressed through modernised client-oriented administration and simpler, transparent rules.

questions.answer: complexity raises compliance costs which encourages evasion and avoidance|complex rules grow the underground economy
questions.explanation: Complexity makes correct calculation costly, encouraging unreported transactions (evasion) and demand for shelters (avoidance), shrinking revenue.
